lines.chapter_title: Opening: The Five-Minute Test
lines.text: For five minutes, you've been chatting with two people. Both of their replies seem completely normal. Sometimes a bit of small talk, sometimes a joke, sometimes a personal question. But only one of them is human. The other is an AI. Now you have to decide which one is the person.
lines.visual: C0-01a: two chat windows A/B, normal replies arrive in both; 5:00 timer; cursor hovers between A and B | C0-01b: cursor hesitates between A and B

lines.chapter_title: Opening: The Five-Minute Test
lines.text: In one experiment, when GPT-4.5 was told to talk like an ordinary young person, people took it for the human 73 percent of the time. And here's the surprising part. When those special instructions were removed, that rate fell to 36 percent.
lines.visual: C0-02a: half-mask slides over window B; marbles drop into the "human?" jar to 73 of 100 | C0-02b: mask lifted away, jar drains to 36

lines.chapter_title: Opening: The Five-Minute Test
lines.text: In other words, it wasn't just the machine's answers. Its way of talking was shaping our decision too. But there's a difference here that's easy to miss. Taking a machine for a human, and that machine actually thinking, are not the same thing.
lines.visual: C0-03a: window B's bubble style and slang emoji glow: the way of talking decides | C0-03b: pull back: the laptop is only a surface; behind it a closed unlit box

lines.chapter_title: Opening: The Five-Minute Test
lines.text: So how do we test whether a machine is only imitating well, whether it understands something, or whether anything is really being experienced inside it? Searching for an answer, we'll travel to an old idea, an extraordinary move in the game of Go, and a locked room.
lines.visual: C0-04a: mask / folded map / lit window line up on the desk: imitate, understand, experience | C0-04b: three 3-4 s glimpses: typed 1950 page, one Go stone landing, a locked door with a slip under it

lines.chapter_title: First Question: How Do You Test Thinking?
lines.text: In 1950, the mathematician Alan Turing wrote a paper. It begins with a simple question: can machines think? But he quickly realises that first we'd have to agree on what "thinking" even means. And people could argue about that definition for years.
lines.visual: C1-01a: framed print of Turing (aged 16) on a desk; a journal page types "Can machines think?" | C1-01b: dictionary entry "think" branches into crossed-out alternatives

lines.chapter_title: First Question: How Do You Test Thinking?
lines.text: So Turing takes a different route. Imagine a person who talks with two others only through written messages. On the other side are a human and a machine, but he isn't told which is which. After the conversation, he has to guess which one is the human.
lines.visual: C1-02a: three-room layout from above: judge at teleprinter, wall with slot, doors A and B | C1-02b: behind the doors (only we see): a person / a 1950 machine cabinet; tape goes red and teal

lines.chapter_title: First Question: How Do You Test Thinking?
lines.text: Today we call this idea the Turing test. It isn't a test of looking inside the machine. It judges its behaviour from the outside: in a conversation, can we tell it apart from a human?
lines.visual: C1-03a: judge side: only tape out of a slot; the wall stays shut

lines.chapter_title: First Question: How Do You Test Thinking?
lines.text: That had a real advantage. Instead of fighting over a definition of thinking that nobody agrees on, you could ask a question you can actually observe. But that is also exactly where the test's limit begins. Sounding human is not proof of understanding on the inside.
lines.visual: C1-04a: argument over a word fades; the judge simply circles A or B (observable) | C1-04b: camera tries to pass through the wall and stops at the plaster

lines.chapter_title: First Question: How Do You Test Thinking?
lines.text: Think back to a viva, the spoken exam. If a student gives the right answer, the teacher may be satisfied. But sometimes the very next question reveals that the answer was memorised, not understood. With machines, this same difference is going to matter.
lines.visual: C1-05a: viva: examiner and student (backs), first answer card ticked | C1-05b: next question: the answer page lifts out of a textbook, identical: memorised | C1-05c: SSEM replica photo (credited) — machines enter the same question

lines.chapter_title: Second Question: Can a Machine Create Something New?
lines.text: The roots of this doubt go back even before Turing. In 1843, Ada Lovelace wrote about Charles Babbage's proposed machine, the Analytical Engine. It was a plan for a kind of computer that was never finished, but its possibilities were astonishing.
lines.visual: C2-01a: Lovelace portrait (credited); Engine trial piece (credited) | C2-01b: Engine drawings with blank unbuilt parts

lines.chapter_title: Second Question: Can a Machine Create Something New?
lines.text: Ada added an important word of caution: the machine makes no claim to create anything new on its own. It can only do what we know how to tell it to do. You still hear this objection today, that a computer, in the end, only runs the rules a human gave it.
lines.visual: C2-02a: punched cards in -> brass mechanism -> output exactly the punched pattern (red thread) | C2-02b: the mechanism repeats, unchanged

lines.chapter_title: Second Question: Can a Machine Create Something New?
lines.text: Turing took this objection seriously. Part of his answer was that we don't need to write out every possible answer for the machine in advance. Why not build a machine that learns like a child, makes mistakes, and changes its behaviour with experience?
lines.visual: C2-03a: marble run of brass flaps: miss, adjust, nearer, lands

lines.chapter_title: Second Question: Can a Machine Create Something New?
lines.text: Today that idea sounds ordinary, but it changes the whole debate. The question is no longer which answer the programmer wrote. The question becomes what a machine, after learning, can do that even the people who built it didn't expect.
lines.visual: C2-04a: blueprint shows one route; the marble takes a better route it never drew (red where different)

lines.chapter_title: Second Question: Can a Machine Create Something New?
lines.text: And then, during a game, a moment came that made some of the world's best experts stop and stare. But to understand it, we first need to see the difference between two very different kinds of computer.
lines.visual: C2-05a: marble drops into a cup that becomes a game piece; down the table: tall cabinet vs a board

lines.chapter_title: Third Question: A Move Nobody Expected
lines.text: In 1997, IBM's computer Deep Blue defeated the world chess champion, Garry Kasparov, in a match. It checked possible moves at enormous speed and weighed up what each one would gain or lose. It was a huge achievement in computing.
lines.visual: C3-01a: Deep Blue cabinet photo (credited) | C3-01b: from one chess position a vast fan of faint ghost futures branches, each scored

lines.chapter_title: Third Question: A Move Nobody Expected
lines.text: In 2016, the contest reached a different game: Go. Lee Sedol, one of South Korea's greatest players, sat down across from AlphaGo, a system built by Google DeepMind. On Go's simple-looking board there are so many possibilities that judging every move just by counting them all is practically impossible.
lines.visual: C3-02a: Lee Sedol photo (credited); quiet match room, the kaya board | C3-02b: ghost stones flicker on every one of 361 points, more and more

lines.chapter_title: Third Question: A Move Nobody Expected
lines.text: AlphaGo learned from games played by expert humans, and then kept improving by playing huge numbers of games against itself. So it wasn't just reading from a list of moves written in advance. Through experience, it built up a sense of which decision works best in which situation.
lines.visual: C3-03a: thousands of faint expert games stream across the board and settle | C3-03b: the board plays itself, games flashing faster

lines.chapter_title: Third Question: A Move Nobody Expected
lines.text: In the second game, AlphaGo played its thirty-seventh move. Today it's remembered as "Move 37". The move was so unusual that the commentators couldn't immediately tell whether it was a mistake, or part of some far-sighted plan.
lines.visual: C3-04a: real Game 2 position; ONE black stone lands on the fifth line (Move 37), red rim | C3-04b: hold on the single stone; nobody moves

lines.chapter_title: Third Question: A Move Nobody Expected
lines.text: According to DeepMind, judging by the data from human games, the chance of a human playing that move was about one in ten thousand. But as the game went on, the move's importance began to show. In the end, AlphaGo won that game, and took the whole series four games to one.
lines.visual: C3-05a: the stone among 10,000 grey grains | C3-05b: soft light spreads from the stone to the group it later supports; stones in a bowl 4-1

lines.chapter_title: Third Question: A Move Nobody Expected
lines.text: This moment isn't memorable because a machine beat a human. What matters is that a learning system chose a strategy that was different from both the habits and the expectations of human experts.
lines.visual: C3-06a: teal ghost stones where experts would play vs the red machine stone elsewhere

lines.chapter_title: Third Question: A Move Nobody Expected
lines.text: So, is Ada Lovelace's objection settled? Not completely. It did show that machines can produce results we never wrote out for them step by step. But playing a new and winning move is not final proof of understanding that move.
lines.visual: C3-07a: Lovelace print slides in beside the board; the board gives no sign of why

lines.chapter_title: Fourth Question: The Chinese Room
lines.text: In 1980, the philosopher John Searle explained this same objection with a memorable example. Imagine you're locked inside a room. You don't know a single word of Chinese. To you, sentences written in Chinese are just strange marks.
lines.visual: C4-01a: Searle photo (credited) | C4-01b: locked door; inside a man at a desk under a bare bulb; a slip of Chinese seen as strange marks

lines.chapter_title: Fourth Question: The Chinese Room
lines.text: A slip of paper comes in under the door. Something is written on it in Chinese. You have a thick book of instructions: if you see marks like these, write these marks in reply and pass them back.
lines.visual: C4-02a: a slip slides in under the door (key still) | C4-02b: he matches the marks in a thick rulebook and copies the shown marks in red ink

lines.chapter_title: Fourth Question: The Chinese Room
lines.text: You follow the book carefully, step by step. Outside, the Chinese speakers get such fitting replies that they believe someone inside the room knows Chinese.
lines.visual: C4-03a: reply pushed out; outside the reader nods, another slip comes in

lines.chapter_title: Fourth Question: The Chinese Room
lines.text: But nothing about you has changed. You don't know what the incoming note means, or what your own reply means. You followed the rules perfectly, but you never understood the language. That was Searle's question: is arranging symbols according to rules the same as understanding?
lines.visual: C4-04a: nothing about him has changed; his reply still marks to him | C4-04b: correct reply slip beside his blank notebook

lines.chapter_title: Fourth Question: The Chinese Room
lines.text: One famous reply came back. Maybe the person inside the room doesn't understand, but the whole system does: the person, the book, the rules, and all of them working together. Searle disagreed. He said that even if the person memorised every instruction, he still wouldn't know what the Chinese means.
lines.visual: C4-05a: top-down: chalk circle drawn around man + book + baskets | C4-05b: pages fly into the man; walls fold away; he answers alone, marks still marks

lines.chapter_title: Fourth Question: The Chinese Room
lines.text: This debate still hasn't fully ended, and neither side can settle it overnight. But Searle's example at least reminds us that there can be a gap between an answer that looks right and understanding on the inside.
lines.visual: C4-06a: correct reply on one side, empty space on the other, a thin line between

lines.chapter_title: Fourth Question: The Chinese Room
lines.text: But now a new question comes up. Are today's AI systems also just repeating the rules of some enormous book? Or, while they learn, does some other way of organising information take shape inside them?
lines.visual: C4-07a: rulebook pages rise, multiply and blur into a lattice of connections

lines.chapter_title: Fifth Question: A Map Inside the Machine
lines.text: To test this, researchers turned to a small game. The game is called Othello. Black and white pieces are placed on a board, and with every new move, the pieces keep changing.
lines.visual: C5-01a: real Othello board: a disc placed, a row flips; again

lines.chapter_title: Fifth Question: A Map Inside the Machine
lines.text: The researchers trained a small GPT-like model on sequences of moves from games. It was never shown a picture of the board, and it wasn't taught the rules of the game separately. All it had was the sequence of moves, and its job was to predict the next legal move.
lines.visual: C5-02a: board covered; a paper tape of move codes feeds a sealed dark-glass box | C5-02b: next legal move comes out of the box

lines.chapter_title: Fifth Question: A Map Inside the Machine
lines.text: After plenty of practice, the model got very good at its predictions. Now the real question was this: was it just memorising common move sequences, or did it somehow also know where the pieces were on the board at that moment?
lines.visual: C5-03a: the box keeps predicting; at the glass: stack of memorised strips, or a board?

lines.chapter_title: Fifth Question: A Map Inside the Machine
lines.text: The researchers examined its internal activity. They found evidence that something like a map of the current board was forming inside the model. Information about where each piece might be was there, inside its calculations.
lines.visual: C5-04a: probe passes the glass; an 8x8 grid of glowing cells emerges in the activity, matching the real board

lines.chapter_title: Fifth Question: A Map Inside the Machine
lines.text: Then they ran another test. They artificially changed the model's internal information about the board, as if one square had been flipped. As a result, the model's predictions for the next moves changed too, to match the altered board.
lines.visual: C5-05a: light tweezers flip ONE inner cell (red) (key still) | C5-05b: the predicted next move changes to fit the altered board

lines.chapter_title: Fifth Question: A Map Inside the Machine
lines.text: That strengthened the case that the internal map wasn't just some unimportant side effect. The model was using it to make its next decision. In a small, limited world, it had learned to organise information in a way nobody taught it directly from outside.
lines.visual: C5-06a: inner map lights as the model chooses; pull back to the box on the table

lines.chapter_title: Fifth Question: A Map Inside the Machine
lines.text: But caution is needed here. A small Othello board is not the real world. And evidence of an internal map is not proof of full, humanlike understanding. Still, this result does weaken the simple picture of a machine that only repeats ready-made sentences.
lines.visual: C5-07a: tiny Othello board before a big window onto the real busy world | C5-07b: a coiled tape of ready-made sentences unspools and falls away

lines.chapter_title: Sixth Question: When the Answer Comes, but the Connection Doesn't
lines.text: On the other hand, some of the mistakes large language models make are interesting too. In a 2023 study, researchers found that a model could state a relationship correctly in one direction, yet fail to recognise the very same relationship the other way round.
lines.visual: C6-01a: drawer A opens: card "mother: B"; drawer B: nothing points back

lines.chapter_title: Sixth Question: When the Answer Comes, but the Connection Doesn't
lines.text: For example, it may know that Tom Cruise's mother is Mary Lee Pfeiffer. But when asked who Mary Lee Pfeiffer's son is, it may not give the right answer. Of course, people forget things too. But a systematic mistake like this makes us ask how the model actually learned the information.
lines.visual: C6-02a: Tom Cruise -> "mother: Mary Lee Pfeiffer"; drawer "Mary Lee Pfeiffer" empty | C6-02b: a person's notebook with one crossed-out entry vs dozens of drawers empty the same way

lines.chapter_title: Sixth Question: When the Answer Comes, but the Connection Doesn't
lines.text: This problem was named the "reversal curse". In related tests, GPT-4 answered questions about celebrities' parents correctly 79 percent of the time in one direction, but in the reverse direction its accuracy fell to 33 percent. This was a specific test of a model checked in 2023. It shouldn't be taken as a permanent limit of every AI.
lines.visual: C6-03a: two stacks of found cards: forward 79 of 100, reverse 33 | C6-03b: small date tag on the drawer

lines.chapter_title: Sixth Question: When the Answer Comes, but the Connection Doesn't
lines.text: Now we have both sides of the picture. In some places, the machine seems to build a working map inside itself, and in others, a simple reversed question confuses it. That's why quick verdicts like "it understands" or "it doesn't understand at all" can go further than the evidence does.
lines.visual: C6-04a: Othello inner map glowing (left) vs empty reverse drawer (right); a level balance

lines.chapter_title: Seventh Question: What Does 73 Percent Really Tell Us?
lines.text: Now let's go back to the experiment we started with. The research first appeared in 2025, and was published in 2026 in the scientific journal PNAS. In the experiment, the person asking questions held a written conversation with a human and an AI at the same time. Then they had to decide which one was the human.
lines.visual: C7-01a: judge's screen with two chats at once; the choice button

lines.chapter_title: Seventh Question: What Does 73 Percent Really Tell Us?
lines.text: When GPT-4.5 was asked to take on the style of a somewhat shy young person who knows internet slang, it was chosen as the human 73 percent of the time. Without that special instruction to adopt the style, the rate was 36 percent. That's why this result reflects not only the model's ability, but also the design of the experiment and its instructions.
lines.visual: C7-02a: persona card clipped to the AI side; jar fills to 73 | C7-02b: card unclipped; jar 36

lines.chapter_title: Seventh Question: What Does 73 Percent Really Tell Us?
lines.text: The researchers also extended the conversations from five minutes to fifteen. In that separate test, with the same kind of persona instructions, GPT-5 was taken for the human about 59 percent of the time. In other words, in some conditions, even more time didn't make it easier for people to tell the difference.
lines.visual: C7-03a: wall clock 5 -> 15 minutes; GPT-5 jar fills to ~59

lines.chapter_title: Seventh Question: What Does 73 Percent Really Tell Us?
lines.text: When people made their decisions, they often paid attention to cues like writing style, the flow of the conversation and personality, rather than deep knowledge or difficult reasoning. Sometimes even a small mistake could make a reply seem more human.
lines.visual: C7-04a: highlights on bubble style, flow, a typo, an emoji; encyclopedia stays closed

lines.chapter_title: Seventh Question: What Does 73 Percent Really Tell Us?
lines.text: So the strong conclusion from this experiment is that some AI systems can imitate a human very convincingly in a short conversation. But on its own, this experiment doesn't tell us how much they understand inside, or whether they feel anything at all.
lines.visual: C7-05a: convincing AI pane in front; behind the laptop the dark sealed box is still closed

lines.chapter_title: Eighth Question: Thinking and Feeling
lines.text: Having come this far, perhaps the hardest distinction comes into view. Solving a problem is one thing. Using information about the world around you is another. And feeling something from the inside, having a personal experience, is a third. These three questions are connected, but they are not the same.
lines.visual: C8-01a: three pools of light on the sill: solved puzzle / folded map / a silhouette feeling the cool air

lines.chapter_title: Eighth Question: Thinking and Feeling
lines.text: For example, an AI can write a beautiful poem about rain. It can say true things about the clouds, the smell of wet earth and the cool breeze. But that doesn't automatically prove it has ever felt the rain.
lines.visual: C8-02a: a teleprinter types a rain poem; real rain streams down the glass; the machine stays dry

lines.chapter_title: Eighth Question: Thinking and Feeling
lines.text: In 2023, nineteen researchers tried to examine the question of consciousness in AI in a more systematic way. They drew a set of indicators from different scientific theories of consciousness, and then looked at where such indicators show up in AI systems.
lines.visual: C8-03a: brass panel of small indicator lamps tagged with theory names; nineteen chairs round a table

lines.chapter_title: Eighth Question: Thinking and Feeling
lines.text: According to that assessment, there was no convincing evidence that the systems they studied at the time were conscious. But the researchers also said that building systems with such indicators in the future doesn't seem impossible in principle. And even finding the indicators would not automatically prove consciousness.
lines.visual: C8-04a: lamps mostly dark; one flickers on, the window stays shut

lines.chapter_title: Eighth Question: Thinking and Feeling
lines.text: So the debate is no longer only about how well a computer can hold a conversation. The question is also what a reliable way to recognise consciousness would even be. When we can't directly see the inner experience of another human being, judging a machine becomes even harder.
lines.visual: C8-05a: two people seen only as lit windows from outside; then a closed door with light under it

lines.chapter_title: Ending: What Evidence Do We Need?
lines.text: So, can machines think? Today, instead of answering in a single word, we can ask the question more clearly. Can a machine hold a humanlike conversation? In some experiments, yes. Can it learn, and build a useful map of the world inside itself? In limited tasks, there is evidence that it can.
lines.visual: C9-01a: door 1 open (chat bubbles beyond), door 2 ajar (inner-map glow)

lines.chapter_title: Ending: What Evidence Do We Need?
lines.text: Does all this mean it understands the way we do, or that it feels anything? On that, there is no decisive agreement yet. Perhaps the better way forward is this: we shouldn't play down what machines achieve, but we also shouldn't draw conclusions from it that we have no evidence for.
lines.visual: C9-02a: door 3 shut, frosted; a balance settles level

lines.chapter_title: Ending: What Evidence Do We Need?
lines.text: And now, the last question is for you. Imagine a machine that talks with you exactly like a human, learns new things, and even corrects its own mistakes. To you, what would be the strongest proof that it is really thinking?
lines.visual: C9-03a: blank card: a pencil writes, errs, erases, writes again | C9-03b: camera stops on the shut door: the question is yours
